extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and researchers in zoology/bryozoan taxonomy
extracted.subtask_description: Use morphological, reproductive, and developmental characters (e.g., anus position, presence of epistome, statoblast morphology, budding patterns) to identify and classify freshwater Polyzoa (bryozoans) into subclasses, orders, and suborders. The page is a textbook-style treatment summarizing diagnostic characters and natural history relevant to taxonomy and identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anus position (Entoprocta vs Ectoprocta)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entoprocta: the anus as well as the mouth is enclosed in the circle of tentacles and the zooecium is not very distinctly separated from the polypide. Ectoprocta: the anus is outside the circle of tentacles and the zooecium can always be distinguished from the polypide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relative position of the anus to the tentacular crown as a primary high-level distinction. Note habitat tendencies: most Entoprocta are marine (but some brackish/freshwater occurrences exist), while most Ectoprocta form permanent colonial communities by budding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of an epistome (Phylactolæmata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phylactolæmata: polypides possess a leaf-shaped organ called an epistome projecting upwards and forwards within the circle of tentacles and between the mouth and the anus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of an epistome is diagnostic of Phylactolæmata; these are freshwater-only taxa. Associated characters: zooecia are not distinct from one another, and dendritic forms often show chitinous partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnolæmata: absence of epistome and zooecial separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gymnolæmata are ectoproctous polyzoa whose polypides have no epistome; the zooecia are in nearly all cases distinctly separated from one another by transverse perforated plates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subclass-level character helps separate Gymnolæmata from Phylactolæmata. Most Gymnolæmata are marine, though some suborders include forms that stray into brackish or fresh water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheilostomata: hinged lip (operculum) and specialized zooecia
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheilostomata (a suborder of Gymnolæmata): zooecia are provided with a 'lip' or lid hinged to the posterior margin of the orifice; the lid closes automatically outside the zooecium or in a special peristome chamber and is pushed open by expanding tentacles. Many zooecia are flattened and some are modified into avicularia and vibracula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hinged operculum (lip) and the presence of modified zooecia (avicularia/vibracula) are key diagnostic features. Cheilostomata are essentially marine but some species occur in estuaries and brackish pools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ctenostomata: collar-like membrane (collar) and zooecial form
rubrics_metrics.description: Ctenostomata: zooecia are provided with a collar-like membrane pleated vertically that closes above the polypide when retracted and is thrust out and expanded into a ring just before tentacles are extruded; zooecia are usually tubular but can be flattened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify ctenostomes by the collar (pleated membrane) and typical tubular zooecia. Some ctenostome divisions include genera that inhabit fresh or brackish water; collar extrusion behavior (ring-shaped expansion) is diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclostomata: lack of lip and collar; tubular zooecia with circular orifices
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyclostomata: zooecia are provided with neither a lip nor a collar-like membrane; they are tubular and usually have circular orifices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combined absence of both operculum and collar, together with tubular zooecia and circular orifices, defines Cyclostomata. These are noted as exclusively marine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statoblast morphology as a classification character
rubrics_metrics.description: Statoblasts are internal buds (masses of cells packed with food-material) enclosed in a capsule with thick horny walls, often surrounded by a 'swim-ring' of horny-walled air-filled chambers; marginal hooked processes may be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The external form of statoblasts is stated to be very important in classification of the Phylactolæmata. Example: Indian genera' statoblasts are flattened with oval/circular outlines. Seasonal production and features such as swim-rings and hooked marginal processes are informative for taxonomy and ecology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resting buds / gemmules (external buds) in Paludicellidæ
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain ctenostomes (e.g., Paludicellidæ) produce external resting buds resembling statoblasts: masses of cells packed with food, protected by a thick horny coat, capable of lying dormant under unfavourable conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These resting buds are taxonomically and ecologically relevant (timing of production differs by climate). Their presence/structure can help distinguish groups (e.g., Paludicellidæ vs Hislopiidæ where no such buds are known).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of reproduction (eggs, budding, asexual dormant bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyzoa reproduce by (i) eggs, (ii) budding (outgrowth of the body-wall forming new polypides), and (iii) asexually produced bodies capable of dormancy (statoblasts/resting buds). Most species are hermaphrodite; reproductive organs are borne on the inner surface of the endocyst, often associated with the funiculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition of reproductive mode (e.g., oviparous vs larva retained; presence of statoblasts) is important for life-history classification and may correlate with habitat (freshwater vs marine) and seasonality. Note fertilization ecology (self vs cross-fertilization uncertain in many species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding pattern and arrangement as diagnostic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Budding order and arrangement differ among groups: freshwater ctenostomes typically produce three buds per zooecium (anterior + two laterals opposite each other) forming crosses; phylactolæmata typically show linear budding with early granddaughter-buds leading to pressed zooecia and irregular lateral budding; some genera (e.g., Victorella) produce additional adventitious buds near the tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the spatial arrangement and timing of buds (daughter vs granddaughter buds, lateral suppression) to distinguish genera and infer colony morphology (cross vs linear series, presence of lateral branches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental and larval characters (egg and statoblast development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development from egg: embryos form a hollow sphere that becomes pear-shaped, acquires cilia, forms polypide(s) by invagination/budding, escapes the zooecium as a ciliated larva, affixes by the broad end and everts the polypide. Statoblast/resting bud development: internal cavity formation, polypide budding within capsule, capsule splitting into valves through which the young emerges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embryological details (larval form, ciliation, mode of escape, inversion of larval tissues, origin of polypide) and statoblast germination behavior (dormancy duration, temperature cues) are diagnostic and have taxonomic/biogeographic significance. Note species-specific variation and references to detailed studies (Allman, Kraepelin, Braem, Oka).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zoarium locomotion and presence of specialized sole
rubrics_metrics.description: Most polyzoan movement is confined to the polypide, but some freshwater genera (Cristatella, Lophopus, Lophopodella, Pectinatella) can move the whole zoarium. Cristatella glides on a specialized mucus-covered 'sole'; other genera may move by alternate expansions and contractions of the base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability of the entire colony to progress and the presence of a creeping sole are discriminating ecological/morphological characters useful in genus-level identification and functional interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary morphological terms as identification vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of technical terms used in classification and description (e.g., brown body, collar, ectocyst, endocyst, epistome, funiculus, gizzard, intertentacular organ, lophophore, parietal muscles, polyparium, polypide, rest bud, statoblast, swim-ring, zoarium, zooecium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent use of these defined terms is necessary for accurate morphological description and comparison. The glossary provides standardized diagnostic language to apply the above criteria correctly (e.g., distinguishing ectocyst vs endocyst when locating reproductive organs or brown bodies).
